submission.natural_language_explanation: The negative pole fires on a token that is only a piece of a word rather than a whole word: it peaks on word-initial or word-medial fragments of rare, technical or foreign words that the tokenizer splits into several tokens (' oc' in ocular, ' mic' in microlensing, ' coch' in cochlear, ' bucc' in buccal, ' hern' in hernia, ' нич' in ничем), on lone letters of non-Latin scripts ('κ', 'σ', ' ه'), and on undecodable bytes ('�'). Tokens that are whole words between word boundaries stay near zero — word-final tokens fire about seven times less often than word-internal ones — so ordinary English text, and rare but single-token technical words such as 'chemotherapy', are predicted inactive; a minority of firings (about a quarter of the scan's active tokens) do land on complete words inside dense citation-heavy technical prose, so the claim is about the class, not every token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
She woke before the sun and put the pot on the stove. The house was cold, so she shut the small window and put on her coat. On the table lay a note from her brother, who had left in the night. She read it twice, then set it down and looked out at the yard. A grey cat walked along the wall and stopped to watch her through the glass. She waved, but the cat did not move.

By six the road was busy. She walked down the hill to the shop, where a young man put bread on the shelf. He said hello and asked about her brother. She told him what the note said, and he said nothing for a while. Then he gave her a bag of rolls and told her to keep the coin.

The rain came at noon. She stood under the roof of the store and watched the drops hit the road. A bus went past with its lights on, and the driver raised a hand. She thought about the fields on the far side of town, where her father had kept a few cows and a horse. The barn was still there, or so the note had said, though the roof was gone.

At one she took the bus to the old house. The path was wet and the gate was open. Inside, the rooms were bare and the floor was dark with damp. She found a box in the back room with her name on it. In the box were a knife, a map, and a small stone she had found as a girl. She put the stone in her pocket and left the box where it was.

The sun came out as she walked back to town. The air was clean and the road was clear. She met the young man again at the shop, and this time she told him she would stay. He smiled and said that was good news. They stood in the door and watched the light move across the hill.

That night she slept in a small room at the back of the shop. The bed was hard and the roof made a sound in the wind, but she slept well. In the morning the young man made tea and they talked about the town and the people in it. He told her the mill had shut and most of the young ones had gone to the city. She said she knew, and that she had been one of them.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Understanding how galaxies assemble remains one of the central problems in modern astrophysics. Numerical simulations of structure formation [1,2] reproduce the observed clustering of matter on large scales, yet the physics of baryons on small scales is still poorly constrained [3]. The cosmic microwave background [4], weak lensing surveys [5], and galaxy redshift surveys [6] together give a consistent picture, although tensions between them persist [7,8].

Stellar physics has advanced alongside cosmology. Observations of the solar photosphere [9] reveal a granulation pattern that models of convection reproduce only in part. Helioseismology constrains the sound speed in the interior, while asteroseismology of red giants [10] now provides ages for thousands of stars. Spectropolarimetry of hot stars measures magnetic fields that drive winds and shape their evolution [11]. Magnetohydrodynamic simulations of the chromospheric layers remain demanding, and comparisons with observation are far from settled [12,13].

Similar problems appear in the laboratory. Plasmas confined by magnetic fields show turbulence and transport that are hard to predict [14]. Spectroscopic measurements of ionised gases [15] can be compared with kinetic models, but the agreement depends on atomic data that are themselves uncertain [16]. Detector arrays now record spectra at rates that were impossible a decade ago, and the resulting archives are large enough to support statistical work on thousands of objects at once.

Theory has its own difficulties. Feedback from stars and black holes is difficult to model, and the resolution of current simulations is far below the scales at which the crucial physics operates [19,20]. Approximate recipes are used in place of a full treatment, and their parameters are adjusted to match observations, which weakens the predictive power of the models. Progress will require both better numerical methods and better data.

The next decade should bring sharper constraints. New facilities will map the sky with unprecedented sensitivity, and the analysis will depend on methods that combine imaging, spectroscopy, and time domain data [17,18]. Whether the current picture survives will depend on how well the systematic errors can be controlled, and on the willingness of the community to share data and software openly.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long-context positive (over 512 tokens) with rare technical words such as spectropolarimetry, asteroseismology and magnetohydrodynamic deep inside, whose fragments the hypothesis predicts fire.
